brief:
# Owner direction (2026-11-21): scale workers up when encoding falls behind

Asked whether the dogfood should refuse 4K HDR re-encodes now (transcodeCores 3), the owner answered instead: "what I'd like to have happen is that we dynamically scale up the amount of pods or something like that as soon as encoding falls behind. I don't know how we do that, if that's done on the operator level, or Kubernetes does that, or we have to do that at the software level." The owner did not approve transcodeCores 3; 4K HDR re-encodes keep stalling on the dogfood until a fix lands.

The lead's reading (product terms; unverified where marked):
- Kubernetes scales: a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (or KEDA) adds and removes worker pods from a metric jellyscale serves on /metrics. jellyscale does not start pods itself (that would tie it to Kubernetes; PRODUCT.md: growing is adding machines; operating stays boring).
- jellyscale's part: (1) a metric that says "encoding is falling behind" (for example: re-encodes running under real time with no helper available, or plays refused for lack of capacity, from JS-153's decision counters and the transcode state); (2) workers that join mid-film and share a slow job already exist (helpers, failover); (3) a worker must be runnable as its own Deployment (the dogfood runs every role in one pod); (4) workers must share the transcode store (the dogfood's is a ReadWriteOnce local volume; S3 or RWX).
- The operator's part: the example manifests (JS-056) could ship the worker Deployment with an autoscaler example; the dogfood would need the shared store (the owner: decide after JS-162/JS-163's figures).
- Limit: a new pod takes seconds to tens of seconds to start (unverified); the viewer who triggers the scale-up may still wait or be refused briefly; a minimum of two workers hides that. Scaling down must not cut a job mid-film (graceful worker stop exists: unverified for this use).
- On the dogfood, extra pods only help on nodes with idle CPUs (k3s-master: 12 nearly idle; JS-163 measures).
tradeoff: Asked whether the dogfood should refuse 4K HDR re-encodes now, the owner answered: "what I'd like to have happen is that we dynamically scale up the amount of pods or something like that as soon as encoding falls behind. I don't know how we do that, if that's done on the operator level, or Kubernetes does that, or we have to do that at the software level." The owner did not approve the interim refusal by configuration. Given up, by the dogfood's viewers: every 4K HDR re-encode keeps stalling with no reason until workers run on other nodes (JS-166), which waits on JS-162's and JS-163's figures and the owner's store decision. Given up, by operators: the autoscaler needs something beside Postgres (a metrics adapter or KEDA), so it stays optional. Given up, by viewers on any cluster at its maximum or while a worker starts: a refusal with a reason (JS-161), not a wait. Unverified when decided: that more workers bring the film to real time end to end; how long a worker pod takes to start; that a worker removed without a replacement costs no stall.
entry: D-043 and D-044 are applied together as written. Autoscaling enters as: JS-164 (one cluster-wide demand number with reasons, because the documented queue signal reads nothing when a play is refused or a job runs slow; pulled out of JS-021 criterion 5), JS-166 (the dogfood runs workers apart on the nodes that can hold the job, after the figures and the owner's store decision; it closes D-038's gap or says it stays open), JS-165 (a worker removed while films play costs no stall, observed first) and JS-057 rewritten (the cluster's own autoscaler on JS-164's number, optional, in the example manifests, then on the dogfood for 14 days). The worker Deployment and the reachable-store check are criteria on JS-056. Kubernetes scales; jellyscale never starts a pod. JS-161's refusal stays the floor and gains a criterion that a job goes to a worker that can hold it; if it would make the dogfood refuse what it stalls on today, the owner is told before that redeploy. Order from 15: JS-162, JS-163, JS-161, JS-164, JS-166, JS-159, JS-158, JS-160, JS-156, JS-041, JS-157, JS-122, JS-075, JS-143, JS-135, JS-136, JS-148, JS-165, JS-150, JS-056, JS-057, then the rest as it was. JS-154 and JS-155 close. Rejected: the autoscaler ahead of the measurements (not shown to fix the film; the dogfood's nodes are fixed); the install and autoscale block ahead of JS-041 and JS-157 (viewer-felt, slipped twice). Data that reopens it: JS-162 or JS-163 showing more workers do not reach real time (JS-166 returns to the product owner and a cheaper output or hardware slice is briefed); JS-164's number above zero on the dogfood with every worker running (the block moves ahead of JS-122); JS-165's observation showing a stall on worker removal.
serves: PRODUCT.md: Play starts in seconds and keeps up. A heavy film uses the whole cluster's processors rather than stalling on one machine while others sit idle. Growing is adding machines; the cluster can grow and shrink with demand by itself. Operating it stays boring; Postgres is the only required service.
